The 4 types of conditionals:
If he works harder, he will succeed.
→ Condition: If clause
→ Result: Main clause
There are 4 types of conditionals:
a) Zero conditional / Type zero:
b) Conditional One / type 1:
c) Conditional Two / type 2:
It is often used to give advice.
d) Conditional Three / type 3:
C H A P I T R E 1
Grammar focus
Example: If you heat water, it boils.	–
Structure: If + present simple → present simple	–
Meaning: Habits, facts, and scientific or general truths.	–
Reference: The present	–
Example: If it rains, we will cancel the trip.	–
Structure: If + simple present → will + verb	–
Meaning: Real / possible situations in the future	–
Reference: The future	–
Example: If she left earlier, she wouldn't be late.	–
Structure: If + simple past → would + verb	–
Meaning: Unreal or impossible situations in the present or the future	–
Reference: The present	–
Example: If I hadn't been sick, I would have gone to your party.	–

ةﻮﻄﺨﺑ ةﻮﻄﺧ ..ﻚﺘﯾاﺮﻗ ﻲﻓ
It is often used to express criticism and regret.
Exercise:
A) Charlotte works for an advertising company. She has made some notes about different
products. Use the correct type of if-clauses to advertise the products:
1- Choose a sunspot holiday / have a great time.
…………………………………………………………………………………………
2- Shop at Tasco / save money.
…………………………………………………………………………………………
3- Use Luxider paint / your house looks beautiful.
…………………………………………………………………………………………
B) Amanda is a secretary. She's complaining about her new job and her boss. She wishes
things were different.
Use if-clauses:
1- He gives me too much work / I have to stay late.
…………………………………………………………………………………………
2- He doesn't listen to me / I have to tell him everything twice.
…………………………………………………………………………………………
3- The offices are such a long way from home / I spend so much time on the bus.
…………………………………………………………………………………………
4- There aren't any cafes nearby / I have to take sandwiches.
…………………………………………………………………………………………
Correction:
A)
1 → If you choose a sunspot holiday, you will have a great day.
2 → If you make a shop at Tasco, you will save money.
Structure: If + past perfect → would have + past participle	–
Meaning: Unreal / imaginary situations that didn't happen in the past.	–
Reference: The past	–

B)

2 → If he didn't listen to me, I would have to tell him everything twice.
3 → If the offices were such a long way from home, I would spend so much time on the bus.
4 → If there were not any cafes nearby, I would have to take sandwiches.
NOTES:
→ Advice.
→ Reproach.
→ Obligation.
→ Deduction.
→ Necessity.
→ Absence of necessity.
→ Regret.
He should work harder.	–
He should have worked harder.	–
She must clean the house.	–
She is absent. She must be sick.	–
It's late, I must go home.	–
They needn't turn it off.	–
I should have helped her.	–
